clinicalPearls: Caused by the giant intestinal fluke Fasciolopsis buski, the largest fluke to infect humans, endemic in parts of South and Southeast Asia
Acquired by eating raw aquatic plants such as water caltrop, water chestnut and water spinach on which metacercariae encyst
Light infection is often silent; heavy infection produces epigastric pain, diarrhoea alternating with constipation, nausea and, in children, malnutrition
Very heavy worm burdens can cause intestinal obstruction and a generalised toxic-allergic state with facial and peripheral oedema
Diagnosis is by finding the large operculated eggs in stool, which resemble those of Fasciola
Praziquantel is the treatment of choice and is highly effective
Prevention centres on not eating raw water plants and on improving sanitation, since pigs act as an important reservoir
reference.pathophysiology: Fasciolopsis buski is a large trematode of the small intestine whose life cycle involves freshwater snails and aquatic vegetation. Cercariae released from snails encyst as metacercariae on the surface of water plants; humans and pigs are infected by eating these plants raw or peeling them with the teeth. The larvae excyst in the duodenum and attach to the mucosa of the upper small intestine, where the large flukes cause local inflammation, ulceration and haemorrhage at the attachment sites. Heavy infections mechanically impair digestion and absorption and can obstruct the bowel, while absorption of fluke metabolites is thought to drive a systemic toxic and allergic reaction manifesting as oedema and constitutional upset. Eggs passed in faeces continue the cycle when they reach freshwater.
additionalDifferentials: Fascioliasis (Fasciola hepatica), whose eggs are morphologically similar
Other intestinal fluke infection such as heterophyiasis and metagonimiasis
Peptic ulcer disease or functional dyspepsia
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for the large operculated eggs, with concentration techniques
Careful egg morphometry to distinguish from Fasciola
Full blood count for eosinophilia and anaemia
Serum albumin and nutritional assessment in heavy or paediatric infection
Abdominal imaging if obstruction is suspected
Repeated stool sampling to improve sensitivity
redFlags: Signs of intestinal obstruction from a heavy worm burden
Generalised oedema and ascites indicating a severe toxic-allergic reaction
Profound malnutrition and growth failure in children
reference.prognosis: Most infections respond promptly to anthelmintic treatment with full recovery; heavy infections in malnourished children can be debilitating and occasionally fatal if obstruction or profound protein loss is untreated.
pitfalls: Confusing Fasciolopsis eggs with those of Fasciola and mislocating the disease to the biliary tract
Underestimating worm burden in children presenting mainly with malnutrition
Missing intestinal obstruction as a complication of heavy infection
Overlooking pigs as a reservoir when advising on control measures
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
